2.text: EMBROIDERY. — Skin clothes are ornamented in two ways, — either with

3.text: embroidery or with appliqué work, formed, like a mosaic, of small squares

4.text: of black and white skin cut out for the purpose and sewed together piece by

5.text: piece (see Plate XXI, Fig. 1). In both branches of this ornamental work the

6.text: women of the Chukchee have but little skill, while those of the Koryak and

7.text: of the Russianized Yukaghir display considerable taste and great patience.

8.text: Embroidery is done with the long hair of the reindeer-mane, which is white

9.text: in color. Often it is dyed red with alder-bark. Thin sinew thread is used

10.text: for the same purpose, as are also long narrow strips of soft white leather.

11.text: Koryak women and Russianized native women also use woollen thread and

13.text: The embroidery patterns used by Chukchee women consist of a few very

14.text: simple geometrical figures, chiefly straight lines, crosses, and circles, single or

15.text: double. The circles are said to represent stars. All these figures may be

16.text: seen on various pieces of embroidery (Plate XXI, Figs. 1-4; also Fig. 158, a-c).

17.text: Occasionally they embellish the trimming of the “dry-shoes,” the opening of

18.text: the sleeves, or the backs of women’s frocks, where tassels are fastened.

19.text: The Reindeer Chukchee women embroider the covers of their family

20.text: sledges according to their skill. These covers have around their lower part

21.text: a broad band of leather embroidered with various geometrical designs, and

22.text: trimmed with fringe and red-dyed fur tassels (Fig. 158, a-c).

23.text: The triangles seen in Plate XXI, Fig. 1, and in Fig. 158, c, were said

24.text: to represent mountains; and the zigzag-like lines in Fig. 158, c, were explained

25.text: as rivers. A part of the design in Fig. 158, c, is apparently copied from the

26.text: engraving on the iron spear-points, the pattern of which, as noted before,

28.text: I could not find a single woman able to give full explanations of her

29.text: own patterns; so that, if they ever had a meaning, it is forgotten by this time.

30.text: Above the band on the back part of the cover is fastened a circle about

31.text: twenty-five or thirty centimetres in diameter, covered all over with embroidery.

32.text: This is called “the sun,” the same name which the Lamut women give to the

33.text: round metal breastplates that form part of their festive costumes. This round

34.text: piece clearly represents the sun, which is often embroidered in the middle,

35.text: and is easily recognized by the prominent rays spreading out from the centre

36.text: of the circle (Plate XXI, Figs. 3, 4). The tassels which are sewed on in the

37.text: centre of the sun or all around the disk also represent the rays. The sun is

38.text: surrounded with many concentric circles, which indicate different worlds. In

39.text: some of these worlds are seen flying birds and shining stars. The birds are

40.text: represented by crosses; and stars, by small circles (Plate XXI, Fig. 4). Once

41.text: in a while a sun-picture is replaced by a moon-picture, which is made in white

42.text: or red, and crossed with several diagonal lines.
